paper.title: LLM+P: Empowering Large Language Models with Optimal Planning Proficiency

read_sources.note: Used for metadata, abstract framing, author list, and project/code link.
Read for PDDL background, method assumptions, benchmark domains, Fast Downward setup, result table, robot demonstration, and limitations.
Used to confirm public code and method names for reproducibility.

summary.one_sentence: LLM+P gets reliable plans by making the LLM translate natural language into PDDL and letting a classical planner do the search.
summary.thesis: For long-horizon planning, the LLM should not be the planner when a sound solver exists; it should be the natural-language interface to that solver.
summary.why_it_matters: The paper is a clean neuro-symbolic systems pattern for agents: separate semantic parsing from plan search, keep a domain model explicit, and route correctness through a verifier/planner instead of model plausibility.

prior_state: LLMs produce plausible natural-language plans that often violate action preconditions or world constraints.
Classical planners can produce correct or optimal plans, but require structured domain and problem encodings.
Robot users naturally specify goals in language, not PDDL.
Long-horizon planning domains expose LLM weaknesses that are hidden by short or underspecified tasks.
problem.key_gap: The paper asks whether an LLM can be used as a translation layer into PDDL so a classical planner can provide the actual planning competence.
assumptions: A domain expert provides a fixed PDDL domain file with action preconditions and effects.
The system knows when a user prompt should be handled by the LLM+P pipeline.
A simple example problem and corresponding PDDL problem file are available as in-context supervision.
The LLM-generated PDDL problem file is good enough for the planner, or failures are acceptable as translation failures.

concepts.name: LLM as PDDL translator
concepts.definition: The LLM maps a natural-language planning instance into a structured PDDL problem file rather than directly outputting the plan.

concepts.name: Domain PDDL
concepts.definition: A task-agnostic specification of predicates, actions, preconditions, and effects supplied by a human expert.

concepts.name: Problem PDDL
concepts.definition: The instance-specific objects, initial state, and goal conditions generated by the LLM from the user request.

concepts.name: Fast Downward planner
concepts.definition: The classical planner used to solve generated PDDL instances, with optimal and satisficing aliases in the experiments.

concepts.name: LLM-as-P
concepts.definition: The baseline strategy where the LLM itself directly produces natural-language plans or ToT-style planning search without a symbolic planner.

method.core_idea: Use the LLM for translation into and out of the formal planning language, but use a classical planner for the search and correctness-critical plan generation.
action_grammar: Natural-language problem: user describes initial state and goal.
Domain PDDL: expert-supplied actions, predicates, preconditions, effects, and optional costs.
Context example: one natural-language problem and matching problem PDDL file.
Problem PDDL generation: the LLM writes the objects, init facts, and goal facts for the new task.
Planner call: Fast Downward solves the domain/problem pair with an optimal or satisficing alias.
Plan translation: the LLM converts the symbolic action sequence back to natural language or robot-executable actions.
Failure mode: invalid or missing PDDL facts cause planner failure or unsolvable instances.
steps: Provide a domain PDDL file for the robot planning domain.
Prompt GPT-4 with the new natural-language planning problem plus one demonstration pair of natural language and PDDL.
Ask the model to produce only the problem PDDL.
Feed the domain and generated problem file to Fast Downward.
If a plan is found, translate the PDDL action sequence back to natural language or robot action execution.
Compare against direct LLM planning, in-context direct planning, and Tree-of-Thought-style direct planning.
method.pseudocode:
domain = load_domain_pddl(domain_name)
example = load_example_pair(domain_name)
problem_pddl = llm.translate_to_pddl(user_problem, example, domain_hint)

plan = fast_downward.solve(domain, problem_pddl, alias="seq-opt-fdss-1")
if plan.timeout_or_fail():
    plan = fast_downward.solve(domain, problem_pddl, alias="lama")

answer = llm.translate_plan_to_language(plan)
return answer

claims.statement: LLM+P delegates planning search to a classical planner after an LLM translates a natural-language task into a PDDL problem file.
caveats: The domain PDDL must already exist and encode the action model correctly.

claims.statement: A simple in-context example is crucial because GPT-4 often emits incorrect PDDL without a demonstration pair.
caveats: This is one-shot prompting, not learned semantic parsing; prompt/domain design remains manual.

claims.statement: The benchmark covers seven robot-planning domains with 20 generated tasks per domain.
caveats: The domains come from planning benchmarks and are translated to robot-style descriptions; they are not arbitrary real-world household requests.

claims.statement: Direct LLM planning mostly produces infeasible plans because it fails to track preconditions and spatial constraints.
caveats: The direct-planning baselines are GPT-4 prompting variants, including a Tree-of-Thought adaptation, not every possible LLM planner.

claims.statement: LLM+P with context substantially improves success across most domains, including 90% Blocksworld, 95% optimal / 100% satisficing Grippers, and 85% Storage.
caveats: Floortile remains 0%, and some LLM+P failures are due to mis-specified generated problem files.

claims.statement: In the home tidy-up robot demonstration, LLM+P finds a lower-cost plan than direct LLM planning by exploiting shared path structure.
caveats: This is a single demonstration, not a large real-robot benchmark.

claims.statement: The framework depends on external trigger detection, human-provided domain models, and accurate PDDL translation by the LLM.
caveats: The paper explicitly leaves auto-detecting when to apply LLM+P and reducing human domain-model dependence as future work.

evidence.result: The pipeline asks the LLM to produce a problem PDDL file, feeds it with a human-provided domain PDDL file to a classical planner, then translates the planner output back to natural language.

Without context, GPT-4's PDDL example has made-up predicates and missing initial facts. With a simple natural-language/PDDL example, the sample problem becomes directly solvable. The results section says LLM+P without context fails to produce correct problem PDDL files.

The benchmark contains seven domains borrowed from past International Planning Competitions: Blocksworld, Barman, Floortile, Grippers, Storage, Termes, and Tyreworld, with 20 automatically generated tasks per domain.

The paper reports that LLM-as-P returns natural-language plans for every problem but most are infeasible. It cites failures tracking Blocksworld on/clear predicates, Barman glass-cleaning requirements, spatial constraints in Floortile, Termes, and Storage, and ToT timeouts from many LLM calls.

LLM+P success rates are Barman 20% optimal / 100% satisficing, Blocksworld 90%, Floortile 0%, Grippers 95% optimal / 100% satisficing, Storage 85%, Termes 20%, and Tyreworld 10% optimal / 90% satisficing. Direct LLM and ToT baselines are much lower in the same table.

In the tidy-up task, LLM+P finds an optimal plan with total cost 22 by taking the bottle partway, disposing of the soup can, re-grasping the bottle, and then going to the pantry. LLM-as-P takes the bottle to the pantry first and returns for the soup can, for cost 31.

The method assumes a robot knows when to trigger LLM+P, a domain PDDL file exists, and an example problem/PDDL pair is provided. The conclusion names auto-detecting when to apply LLM+P and reducing dependence on human-provided information as future work.

agent_infra_takeaways: Use LLMs as translators when a sound solver exists. Planning correctness should come from the planner, not from plausible prose.
The action model is infrastructure. Domain PDDL is a contract over capabilities, preconditions, effects, and costs.
Structured intermediate representations make agent failures inspectable: bad plan versus bad translation is a different bug.
One-shot examples can be enough to steer translation, but production systems need validation and repair loops for generated PDDL.
A planner-backed agent needs a router that decides when a task belongs to the planner rather than the general LLM loop.
The same pattern generalizes beyond planning: calculators, compilers, theorem provers, and simulators should own domains where they are sound.
caveats: The domain model is manually supplied; LLM+P does not learn or verify the domain PDDL.
The planner can only be correct with respect to the given domain and problem encoding.
Generated PDDL can omit facts or use wrong predicates, causing planner failure or an invalid plan request.
Floortile remains unsolved in the reported table.
The real-robot demonstration is a single tidy-up scenario.
The paper does not solve when to invoke the planning pipeline automatically.

related_work.title: On the Planning Abilities of LLMs
related_work.note: Both papers argue that direct LLM planning is weak; LLM+P proposes a solver-backed remedy.

related_work.title: Voyager
related_work.note: Voyager improves planning by writing/reusing executable code in Minecraft, while LLM+P routes formal planning to a symbolic solver.

poc.note: No PoC yet - contributions welcome. A useful PoC would translate a tiny Blocks World natural-language instance into PDDL, run a local planner or validator, and translate the plan back to text.
